notes: r10-06 uses union-enum-member-disjointness instead of switch narrowing to avoid repeating r4 control-flow narrowing. r10-10 uses as-const-object-value-union instead of as-const-object-runtime to avoid repeating assertion erasure. r10-11 uses heterogeneous-enum-members instead of literal-union-no-runtime-object to avoid mirroring the regular-enum runtime card.

cards.statement: In `Required<Partial<{ id: number }>>`, `{}` fails assignment.
cards.explanation: Partial makes `id` optional, then Required makes it mandatory again; `{}` lacks the resulting required property.

cards.statement: `Readonly<{ config: { enabled: boolean } }>` makes the nested `enabled` property readonly.
cards.explanation: Readonly changes top-level properties. In this type, `config` cannot be reassigned, but its nested `enabled` property can.
cards.misconception: Readonly recursively freezes nested properties.

cards.statement: `Record<"a" | "b", number>` requires both `a` and `b` keys.
cards.explanation: `Record<"a" | "b", number>` creates a required numeric property for each key in its key union.

cards.statement: `Pick<{ id: number; name: string }, "id">` and `Omit<{ id: number; name: string }, "name">` match.
cards.explanation: Pick retains `id`; Omit removes `name`. Applied to this two-property input, both leave `{ id: number }`.

cards.statement: `Exclude<string | number, string>` and `Extract<string | number, number>` both yield `number`.
cards.explanation: Exclude removes `string` from the union, while Extract keeps `number`; both calculations leave `number`.

cards.statement: Given `string | 0 | null`, `NonNullable` filters out the literal member `0`.
cards.explanation: NonNullable removes `null` and `undefined`, not other falsy values. `NonNullable<string | 0 | null>` remains `string | 0`.
cards.misconception: NonNullable filters every falsy union member.

cards.statement: `Parameters` and `ReturnType` use an overloaded function’s first signature.
cards.explanation: For an overloaded function, both `Parameters<Type>` and `ReturnType<Type>` use the last overload signature.
cards.misconception: Utility types inspect the first overload signature.

cards.statement: `ConstructorParameters<ErrorConstructor>` is `[message?: string]`; `InstanceType<ErrorConstructor>` is `Error`.
cards.explanation: `ConstructorParameters` captures constructor arguments; `InstanceType` describes the constructed object. For `ErrorConstructor`, those are `[message?: string]` and `Error`.

cards.statement: `Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>>` produces `Promise<number>` after one level of unwrapping.
cards.explanation: Awaited recursively unwraps nested promises, so `Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>>` is `number`.
cards.misconception: Awaited unwraps just one Promise layer.

cards.statement: `NoInfer<C>` lets a fallback value widen the `C` inferred from a separate `colors: C[]` argument.
cards.explanation: `NoInfer<C>` blocks the fallback from contributing inference candidates for `C`. The fallback is checked against `C` inferred from the other argument.
cards.misconception: A NoInfer parameter can widen the inferred type argument.

cards.statement: For `(this: Date) => number`, `ThisParameterType` gives `Date | undefined` as the receiver type.
cards.explanation: `ThisParameterType<(this: Date) => number>` is `Date`. `OmitThisParameter` removes the explicit receiver parameter from a function type.
cards.misconception: ThisParameterType adds undefined to an explicit this parameter.

cards.statement: In an object context typed as `M & ThisType<{ x: number }>`, methods see `this.x` as `number`.
cards.explanation: `ThisType<{ x: number }>` marks the contextual `this` type for methods of a suitably typed object; `noImplicitThis` must be enabled.

cards.statement: In `enum E { A = 4, B }`, TypeScript assigns `E.B` the numeric value `5`.
cards.explanation: A numeric enum member after a constant numeric member auto-increments the preceding value, so `B` is `5`.

cards.statement: In `enum E { A = Math.random(), B }`, TypeScript automatically gives `B` the next value.
cards.explanation: An enum member following a computed initializer needs its own initializer. `B` in this declaration produces an error.
cards.misconception: A computed numeric enum member allows the next member to auto-increment.

cards.statement: In `enum E { A = "a", B = A }`, TypeScript assigns `E.B` the string value `"a"`.
cards.explanation: A string enum member can initialize from another string enum member, so `B` receives `A`'s value, `"a"`.

cards.statement: In `enum E { A = "a" }`, `E["a"]` yields the member name `"A"`.
cards.explanation: String enum members get no reverse mapping. The generated enum object has no `"a"` key mapped to `"A"`.
cards.misconception: String enums have the same reverse mapping as numeric enums.

cards.statement: In `enum E { A = "a", B = "b" }`, the member `E.A` can serve as a property type.
cards.explanation: When every member has a literal enum value, each member is also a type; `E.A` can type a property.

cards.statement: For `enum E { A, B }`, TypeScript treats `E.A` and `E.B` as overlapping types.
cards.explanation: For a union enum with distinct literal members, `E.A` and `E.B` are disjoint member types; TypeScript flags impossible comparisons between them.
cards.misconception: Distinct literal enum members overlap in the checker.

cards.statement: A regular `enum` produces a JavaScript object that code can pass to a function.
cards.explanation: A regular enum emits a runtime object with member properties, so it can be passed where an object with compatible properties is expected.

cards.statement: `const enum E { A = 1 }` inlines `E.A` as a value in emitted JavaScript.
cards.explanation: A `const enum` is removed on emit, and references to its members are replaced with their constant values.

cards.statement: With `isolatedModules`, code can reference ambient `const enum` members.
cards.explanation: An ambient `const enum` has no emitted value, and `isolatedModules` rejects member references because single-file transpilation cannot inline them.
cards.misconception: Ambient const enums work with isolatedModules.

cards.statement: `typeof O[keyof typeof O]` widens to `number` for `const O = { Up: 0, Down: 1 } as const`.
cards.explanation: The `as const` object keeps literal property types, so `typeof O[keyof typeof O]` is `0 | 1`, not the wider `number`.
cards.misconception: An as const object still produces a widened number union.

cards.statement: In `enum E { A = 0, B = "b" }`, TypeScript accepts both members.
cards.explanation: TypeScript permits an enum to mix numeric and string members. `A` is numeric and `B` is a string member in this declaration.

cards.statement: With `erasableSyntaxOnly` enabled, TypeScript accepts a regular `enum` declaration.
cards.explanation: `erasableSyntaxOnly` rejects regular enums because they require runtime code generation rather than simple type erasure.
cards.misconception: Enums are erasable TypeScript syntax.

cards.statement: Since TypeScript 6.0, `strict` is enabled by default.
cards.explanation: TypeScript 6.0 changed the `strict` default to `true`, and TypeScript 7.0 retains that default.

cards.statement: The `strict` family includes `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`.
cards.explanation: The `strict` family enables alwaysStrict, noImplicitAny, noImplicitThis, strictBindCallApply, strictBuiltinIteratorReturn, strictFunctionTypes, strictNullChecks, strictPropertyInitialization, and useUnknownInCatchVariables.
cards.misconception: noUncheckedIndexedAccess is enabled by strict.

cards.statement: With `noImplicitThis`, an inner regular function inherits its enclosing class instance as `this`.
cards.explanation: A regular nested function has its own `this`. `noImplicitThis` flags an implicitly `any` `this` rather than inferring the enclosing class instance.
cards.misconception: A regular nested function captures the enclosing class this under noImplicitThis.

cards.statement: With `strictBindCallApply`, `.call` rejects an argument incompatible with its function parameter.
cards.explanation: `strictBindCallApply` checks `.call`, `.bind`, and `.apply` against the target function's argument types; a mismatch produces an error.

cards.statement: With `strictBuiltinIteratorReturn`, a built-in iterator’s return type parameter becomes `undefined`.
cards.explanation: `strictBuiltinIteratorReturn` gives built-in iterators `TReturn` of `undefined` instead of `any`.

cards.statement: With `strictFunctionTypes`, method parameters receive the same check as function property parameters.
cards.explanation: `strictFunctionTypes` applies the stricter parameter check to function syntax, but method syntax remains bivariant.
cards.misconception: strictFunctionTypes applies identically to methods and function properties.

cards.statement: With `strictPropertyInitialization`, `class C { x: string; constructor() {} }` reports an error.
cards.explanation: `strictPropertyInitialization` reports `x` because a required `string` field has neither a property initializer nor an assignment in the constructor.

cards.statement: With `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, `catch (e)` permits `e.message` before a guard.
cards.explanation: `useUnknownInCatchVariables` gives an unannotated catch binding type `unknown`; a guard such as `e instanceof Error` is needed before reading `.message`.
cards.misconception: A catch binding is directly usable as an Error when useUnknownInCatchVariables is on.

cards.statement: With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `obj["x"]` has type `string | undefined` when `obj: Record<string, string>`.
cards.explanation: When a key is present only via an index signature, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` includes `undefined` in the read type to account for a missing value.

cards.statement: With `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `{ p: undefined }` fits `{ p?: string }`.
cards.explanation: `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` distinguishes an absent property from one holding `undefined`; `{ p: undefined }` fails against `{ p?: string }`.
cards.misconception: An optional property implicitly accepts an explicit undefined value under exactOptionalPropertyTypes.

cards.statement: With `noImplicitOverride`, a subclass method overriding a base method requires `override`.
cards.explanation: `noImplicitOverride` requires the `override` modifier when a subclass method replaces one in its base class, helping detect mismatched overrides.

cards.statement: With `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature`, TypeScript directly accepts `obj.key` for an index-only key.
cards.explanation: `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` requires bracket access for a key known only through an index signature; `obj["key"]` is accepted while `obj.key` errors.
cards.misconception: Index-signature-only properties still support dot access under the option.

cards.statement: With `module: nodenext`, a `.ts` file’s module format follows the nearest `package.json` `type` field.
cards.explanation: `module: nodenext` selects ESM for a `.ts` file when the nearest package.json has `"type": "module"`; otherwise that file is CommonJS.

cards.statement: With `moduleResolution: bundler`, relative ESM imports require explicit `.js` extensions.
cards.explanation: `moduleResolution: bundler` supports extensionless relative imports, matching common bundler resolution behavior.
cards.misconception: Bundler resolution requires extensions for ESM relative imports.

cards.statement: With `module: preserve`, TypeScript converts `import = require` into an ESM import in emitted code.
cards.explanation: `module: preserve` keeps each import or export syntax: `import x = require("mod")` emits a `require` call, while ESM imports stay ESM.
cards.misconception: module preserve rewrites CommonJS imports as ESM imports.

cards.statement: Since TypeScript 6.0, `module` defaults to `esnext`.
cards.explanation: TypeScript 6.0 switched the default `module` value to `esnext`, and TypeScript 7.0 kept it.

cards.statement: In TypeScript 7.0, `moduleResolution: node10` can be selected in `tsconfig.json`.
cards.explanation: TypeScript 7.0 rejects `moduleResolution: node10` as a removed option; use `nodenext` or `bundler` instead.
cards.misconception: node10 remains a supported module resolution strategy in TypeScript 7.0.

cards.statement: With `verbatimModuleSyntax`, TypeScript retains `import type` declarations in JavaScript output.
cards.explanation: `verbatimModuleSyntax` drops `import type` declarations from JavaScript output; imports lacking a `type` modifier remain.
cards.misconception: verbatimModuleSyntax preserves type-only imports in JavaScript.

cards.statement: With `isolatedModules`, `export { T }` triggers an error when `T` refers only to a type.
cards.explanation: `isolatedModules` reports value-style exports of names that refer only to types because a single-file transpiler cannot know whether those names exist at runtime.

cards.statement: Since TypeScript 6.0, `paths` mappings work when `baseUrl` is unset.
cards.explanation: `paths` mappings work with `baseUrl` unset; TypeScript 6.0 deprecated `baseUrl` and stopped using it as a lookup root.

cards.statement: A `declare function` in a `.d.ts` file provides a JavaScript implementation.
cards.explanation: A `.d.ts` file describes existing values and types for checking; it emits no JavaScript implementation.
cards.misconception: Declaration files supply runtime implementations.

cards.statement: Since TypeScript 6.0, `types` includes visible `@types` packages by default.
cards.explanation: From TypeScript 6.0 onward, `types` defaults to `[]`. Visible `@types` packages enter the global scope when selected in `types`.
cards.misconception: All installed @types packages are automatically included in the global scope by default.

cards.statement: With `skipLibCheck`, TypeScript checks source references to declarations despite skipping their full `.d.ts` check.
cards.explanation: `skipLibCheck` skips full checking of declaration files; TypeScript still checks types referred to by application source.

cards.statement: A `declare global` block inside a module can extend a global interface.
cards.explanation: Global augmentation lets a module add to global declarations, such as the `Array` interface; it follows the same merge rules as module augmentation.
